hello.title: Hello, Elixir
hello.summary: Write your first Elixir script, print text with IO.puts, join strings and add comments.
hello.lesson.0: Elixir is a friendly language for building reliable programs. You write a program in a **script** file that ends in `.exs`, for example `hello.exs`. In a terminal, the command `elixir hello.exs` runs it.
hello.lesson.2: `IO.puts` prints text and then starts a new line. `IO` is a **module** (a group of functions) and `puts` is a function inside it. The dot `.` connects the module and the function. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, Elixir!"`, is a **string**.
hello.lesson.4: The program runs from top to bottom, one line after the other. `IO.puts` can also print numbers and the result of a calculation, like `2 + 3`.
hello.lesson.6: The operator `<>` joins two strings into one. With `=` you give a value a name: `name = "Ada"`. Later you write `name` to use the value. Such a name is called a **variable**.
hello.lesson.8: `IO.inspect` shows a value the way Elixir writes it in code. A string appears with its quotes, so you can see what kind of value it is. This helps a lot when you look for mistakes.
hello.lesson.10: A line that starts with `#` is a **comment**. Elixir ignores it. You can use `#` to switch off a line of code without deleting it.
hello.lesson.12: You can leave out the parentheses: `IO.puts "Hi"` works too. In this course you always write them, because it makes the code easier to read.
hello.card.1: `IO.puts("Hi")` prints text and a new line
hello-1.explain: You start a script with the command `elixir` followed by the file name.
hello-2.explain: `<>` joins the two strings. The space at the end of `"Good "` stays in the result.
hello-3.explain: `word` holds the string `"fun"`. `<>` adds it to the end of `"Elixir is "`.
hello-4.statement: `IO.puts` starts a new line after the text it prints.
hello-4.explain: That is why two calls of `IO.puts` print their texts on two separate lines.

hello-5.explain: The function is called `puts`. The module `IO` has no functions called `print`, `echo` or `println`.

hello-6.explain: In Elixir, `<>` joins strings. `+` only works with numbers.

hello-7.explain: `IO.puts` gets one string: `"Hi, "` joined with `name` by `<>`.

hello-8.explain: A variable must have a value before you use it: first `name`, then `greeting`, then print.

basics.title: Basic types
basics.summary: Work with integers, floats, atoms, booleans and strings, and put values into strings with interpolation.
basics.lesson.0: Elixir has two kinds of numbers. An **integer** is a whole number like `7`. A **float** is a number with a decimal point like `3.5`. You calculate with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`.
basics.lesson.2: The operator `/` always gives a float, even when the result is whole: `10 / 2` is `5.0`. For whole-number division use `div(a, b)`. `rem(a, b)` gives the rest (the **remainder**) of that division.
basics.lesson.5: An **atom** is a name that stands for itself. It starts with a colon, like `:ok` or `:error`. The **booleans** `true` and `false` are the answers to questions like `5 > 3`. You compare with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`, and you combine with `and`, `or` and `not`. Functions like `is_integer` and `is_float` check the type of a value.
basics.lesson.8: Inside a string, `#{...}` puts a value into the text. This is called **interpolation**. Between the braces you can write any expression, for example `age + 1`.
basics.lesson.10: The module `String` has many functions for text. `String.length` counts the characters and `String.upcase` turns all letters into capitals.
basics.lesson.12: `String.upcase(word)` returns a new string. The value of `word` does not change. In Elixir, values never change; you always create new ones.
basics.card.3: `"Hi #{name}"` puts a value into a string
basics-1.explain: `div` divides and drops the rest: 20 divided by 6 is 3, rest 2.
basics-2.explain: 6 fits into 20 three times (18). The remainder is 20 - 18 = 2.
basics-3.explain: `/` always returns a float, so the result is `3.0`, not `3`.
basics-4.prompt: Which of these is an atom?
basics-4.explain: An atom starts with a colon. `"ok"` is a string and `ok` is a variable name.
basics-5.explain: `#{name}` is replaced by the value of `name`. `IO.puts` prints a string without quotes.
basics-6.explain: `10 / 2` is `5.0`. The operator `/` always gives a float.
basics-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 2.
basics-7.explain: 17 divided by 5 is 3, rest 2. `rem` gives the rest; `div` would give 3.
basics-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints Total: 12.
basics-8.explain: Interpolation in Elixir uses `#{...}`. The other options are printed as plain text.
basics-9.prompt: Print the length of the string `word` plus 1.
basics-9.explain: `String.length(word)` returns a number, so you add 1 with `+`. `<>` only joins strings.
basics-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 6.
basics-10.explain: Each line uses the variable from the line before: `div(10, 3)` is 3, and 3 * 2 is 6.

basics-12.explain: `<>` only joins strings, and `age + 1` is a number. Write `IO.puts("Next: #{age + 1}")`.
matching.title: Pattern matching
matching.summary: Use the match operator to unpack tuples and lists, ignore values and keep values with the pin operator.
matching.lesson.0: In Elixir, `=` is the **match operator**. Elixir makes the left side match the right side. When the left side is a variable, the variable gets the value. Because it is a match, `5 = x` is also valid when `x` is 5. When the two sides do not match, the program stops with a `MatchError`.
matching.lesson.3: A **tuple** groups a fixed number of values in curly braces: `{"Ada", 36}`. With a match you take a tuple apart and give each part a name.
matching.lesson.5: Many functions return tuples like `{:ok, value}` or `{:error, reason}`. An atom in a pattern must be exactly equal, so `{:ok, result}` only matches a tuple that starts with `:ok`.
matching.lesson.8: A **list** holds values in square brackets: `[10, 20, 30]`. A list pattern matches only a list with the same number of items. The underscore `_` matches any value and ignores it.
matching.lesson.11: You can match a variable again: `x = 2` gives `x` a new value. If you want to use the current value of `x` instead, put the **pin operator** `^` in front of it. Then `^x = 2` only checks that the value is 2.
matching.lesson.13: A pinned variable never gets a new value. If `x` is 2, then `^x = 3` raises a `MatchError`.
matching-1.explain: The match gives `a` the value 3 and `b` the value 4. 3 * 4 is 12.
matching-3.explain: The right side is calculated first: 10 + 5 is 15. Then `x` gets the new value 15.
matching-4.explain: `^x` keeps the value 4, and 4 does not match 5.
matching-5.explain: `status` matches the first element of the tuple, the atom `:error`.
matching-6.explain: The pattern `[a, b]` has two items, but the list has three. The lengths must be equal.
matching-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 6.
matching-7.explain: The variable `middle` gets the second item, 6. `^middle` needs a value that already exists, and `:middle` is an atom.
matching-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 3.
matching-8.explain: The right side is a tuple with two values, so the pattern must be a tuple with two variables.
matching-9.explain: The pattern goes on the left of `=` and the value on the right. Both are tuples with two elements.
matching-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 22.
matching-10.explain: `x` is 1, so `y` is 2. Then `x` gets the new value 20. 20 + 2 is 22.

matching-11.pairs.2: uses the current value of x

conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program choose with if and else, case, cond and guards with when.
conditions.lesson.0: `if` runs code only when a condition is true. The code goes between `do` and `end`. The part after `else` runs when the condition is not true. Only `false` and `nil` (which means "no value") count as false; every other value counts as true, also `0` and `""`.
conditions.lesson.2: `if` returns a value, so you can store its result in a variable. For short cases there is a one-line form with `do:` and `else:`. Note the commas.
conditions.lesson.5: `case` compares a value with several **patterns**, from top to bottom. The first pattern that matches wins, and the code after its arrow `->` runs. Variables in the pattern get their values from the match.
conditions.lesson.8: `cond` checks several conditions from top to bottom and runs the code of the first one that is true. The last condition is often `true`, which always matches. It works like a final `else`.
conditions.lesson.11: A **guard** adds a condition to a pattern with the keyword `when`. The pattern matches only when the guard is also true. The pattern `_` at the end catches every other value.
conditions.lesson.13: If no pattern of a `case` matches, the program stops with a `CaseClauseError`. If no condition of a `cond` is true, it stops with a `CondClauseError`. Add `_ ->` or `true ->` at the end to avoid this.
conditions-1.explain: `rem(7, 2)` is 1, so the condition is false and the `else` part runs.
conditions-2.explain: 15 is not greater than 25, but it is greater than 10. The first true condition wins.
conditions-4.prompt: Which values count as false in an `if`?
conditions-4.explain: In Elixir, only `false` and `nil` are false. `0` and `""` count as true.
conditions-5.explain: The guard `x > 0` is false for 0, so the next pattern `0` matches.
conditions-6.explain: 5 is not greater than 10, so the `else:` part runs and prints `small`.
conditions-7.prompt: Complete the code so the last line catches every other case.
conditions-7.explain: In `cond`, the condition `true` is always true, so it works as the final case. `_` is only for patterns in `case`.
conditions-8.prompt: Complete the guard so the code prints big.
conditions-8.explain: A guard starts with the keyword `when`.
conditions-9.prompt: Write a one-line `if` that gives `"yes"` when `x > 3` and `"no"` otherwise.
conditions-9.explain: The one-line form is `if condition, do: value, else: value`.
conditions-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so a score of 95 prints A, 85 prints B and 50 prints C.
conditions-10.explain: `cond` takes the first true condition. With `score >= 80` first, 95 would print B, and `true` must come last.

functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write anonymous functions, named functions in modules, and chain calls with the pipe operator.
functions.lesson.0: A function takes values (its **arguments**) and returns a result. `fn x -> x * 2 end` is an **anonymous function**: it has no name, but you can store it in a variable. To call it, write a dot before the parentheses: `double.(4)`.
functions.lesson.2: Arguments are separated by commas. The function returns the value of its last expression; Elixir has no `return` keyword.
functions.lesson.5: Named functions live in a **module**. `defmodule` creates the module and `def` defines a function inside it. Module names start with a capital letter. You call the function with the module name and a dot, without an extra dot before the parentheses: `Math.square(5)`.
functions.lesson.7: A short function fits on one line with `, do:`. A function can have several **clauses** with different patterns. Elixir tries them from top to bottom and runs the first one that matches. Guards with `when` work here too.
functions.lesson.10: A function is known by its name and its number of arguments, the **arity**. You write it as `square/1` or `add/2`. `defp` instead of `def` makes a **private** function that only the same module can call.
functions.lesson.12: The **pipe operator** `|>` takes the result on its left and passes it as the first argument to the function on its right. `"hi" |> String.upcase()` is the same as `String.upcase("hi")`. A chain of pipes reads from top to bottom.
functions.card.2: Clauses are tried from top to bottom
functions-1.explain: `triple.(5)` calls the function with `x` = 5, and 5 * 3 is 15.
functions-2.explain: `price` is 4 and `count` is 3. The function returns 4 * 3.
functions-3.explain: The pipe passes 10 as the first argument: `div(10, 3)` is 3. Then 3 goes into `IO.puts`.

functions-6.explain: The pipe passes the value on its left as the first argument. Both give `"ABC"`.

functions-7.explain: Named functions in a module are defined with `def`.

collections.title: Lists and maps
collections.summary: Store many values in lists and maps, split lists into head and tail, and use keyword lists and Map functions.
collections.lesson.0: A list keeps values in order. `++` joins two lists, `--` removes items, and `length` counts the items. To print a list, use `IO.inspect`; `IO.puts` is only for text and numbers.
collections.lesson.3: The pattern `[head | tail]` splits a list. `head` gets the first item and `tail` gets a list with all the other items. The same `|` also adds an item to the front: `[5 | tail]`. The tail of a one-item list is the empty list `[]`, and `[]` itself does not match `[head | tail]`.
collections.lesson.6: A **map** stores values under **keys**: `%{name: "Ada", age: 36}`. When the keys are atoms, you read a value with `user.name` or `user[:name]`. For a missing key, `user[:email]` gives `nil`, while `user.email` stops with a `KeyError`.
collections.lesson.8: You can match maps too. A map pattern only needs the keys it names, so `%{name: name} = user` takes the name out of `user`, even though `user` also has the key `:age`.
collections.lesson.9: `Map.put` returns a new map with one more key; the old map does not change. `Map.get(map, key, default)` returns the default when the key is missing. `%{map | key: value}` returns a copy with a new value for a key that already exists.
collections.lesson.12: A **keyword list** is a list of pairs with atom keys, written `[size: 10, color: "red"]`. It is a short way to write `[{:size, 10}, {:color, "red"}]`. Functions often take options in this form. You read a value with `opts[:color]`.
collections-1.explain: `_` ignores the first item, 3. `rest` gets the list of the other items.
collections-2.explain: `++` joins the lists into `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`, which has 5 items.

collections-5.explain: `[item | list]` puts a new item in front of a list.

enum.title: Enum and ranges
enum.summary: Transform lists and ranges with Enum.map, filter, reduce and sum, and write short functions with the capture operator.
enum.lesson.0: The module `Enum` has functions that work with every item of a list. `Enum.map(list, function)` calls the function for each item and returns a new list with the results.
enum.lesson.2: `Enum.filter` keeps only the items for which the function returns `true`. `Enum.sum` adds all items, `Enum.max` finds the largest one and `Enum.count` counts them.
enum.lesson.5: A **range** like `1..5` stands for all whole numbers from 1 to 5, including both ends. `Enum` functions work with ranges too. `Enum.to_list` turns a range into a list.
enum.lesson.7: `Enum.reduce(list, start, function)` combines all items into one value. The function gets an item and the **accumulator** `acc`, the result so far. It returns the new result. `acc` starts with the value `start`.
enum.lesson.10: The **capture operator** `&` writes short functions. In `&(&1 * 2)`, `&1` is the first argument, so it means `fn x -> x * 2 end`. `&String.upcase/1` turns the named function `String.upcase` with arity 1 into a function value.
enum.lesson.12: `Enum` functions take the list as their first argument, so they work well with the pipe. This pipeline keeps the even numbers from 1 to 10, squares them and adds them up.
enum.card.2: `Enum.reduce(list, 0, fn x, acc -> x + acc end)`
enum-1.explain: `Enum.map` adds 1 to every item and returns the new list.
enum-2.explain: The anonymous function needs `end`: `Enum.map(nums, fn n -> n * 2 end)`.
enum-3.explain: Only 8 and 6 are greater than 4, so the filtered list has 2 items.
enum-5.explain: A range includes both ends, so `2..5` has the numbers 2, 3, 4 and 5.
enum-7.explain: `filter` keeps the items where the function is true. `rem(n, 2) == 0` is true for the even numbers, so it prints `[2, 4]`.

recursion.title: Recursion
recursion.summary: Repeat work with functions that call themselves, stop them with a base case, and carry results in an accumulator.
recursion.lesson.0: Elixir has no `while` loop. To repeat work, a function calls itself. This is called **recursion**. Every recursive function needs a **base case**: a clause that stops without calling itself again.
recursion.lesson.2: `down(3)` prints 3 and calls `down(2)`, which prints 2 and calls `down(1)`, and so on. `down(0)` matches the first clause, the base case, so the calls stop there.
recursion.lesson.4: With `[head | tail]` a function handles the first item and leaves the rest of the list to a recursive call. The base case is the empty list `[]`.
recursion.lesson.6: Step by step: `sum([4, 5, 6])` is `4 + sum([5, 6])`, which is `4 + 5 + sum([6])`, which is `4 + 5 + 6 + sum([])`. `sum([])` is 0, so the result is 15.
recursion.lesson.7: A recursive function can also build a new list. Here each call puts the doubled head in front of the result for the tail.
recursion.lesson.10: An **accumulator** is an extra argument that carries the result so far. A public function starts it with a first value and a private helper made with `defp` does the work. When the list is empty, the helper returns the accumulator.
recursion.lesson.12: Put the base case before the general clause, and make sure each call gets closer to it. Without a base case that matches, the function never stops.
recursion.lesson.13: In real programs, `Enum.sum`, `Enum.map` and `Enum.count` do this work for you. Inside, they use the same idea: recursion.
recursion-2.explain: The second clause drops the head until one item is left. `[x]` then matches the list `[8]`.
recursion-3.explain: Each call multiplies by 2, five times: 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 * 2 * 1 is 32.
recursion-4.prompt: What is the base case of a recursive function?
recursion-4.options.0: The clause that returns without calling the function again
recursion-4.options.1: The first function in a module
recursion-4.options.2: The largest input the function accepts
recursion-4.options.3: The call that starts the recursion
recursion-4.explain: The base case stops the recursion. Without it, the function would call itself forever.
recursion-5.explain: Each call compares the head with the biggest item of the tail and keeps the larger one, so the result is 9.
recursion-6.explain: `len` adds 1 for each item and ignores the values, so it prints the length 4.
